note: Student-facing activity content. Answers live in teacher-keys.json and are never written into student handouts.

activities.title: Break It: Biology
activities.description: Students break three -LOGY words into parts, record what each part means, and explain why the three fields of study are different.

blocks.text: Every word below ends with the same word part. Break each word apart, write what each piece means, and then say what the whole word means in your own words.

blocks.label: All three words end in LOGY. What does that tell you about all three?
A scientist studies how a drought changes which animals stay in a prairie. Which of the three words names that work? How do you know?

blocks.a: Say what LOGY means in your own words.
blocks.c: Explain how the first word part changes what is being studied.
blocks.e: Name one more word you know that ends in LOGY. What do you think it studies?

activities.title: Build It: Word-Part Cards
activities.description: Students cut apart ten word-part cards, combine them into real science terms, and record the science meaning of each term they build.

blocks.text: Cut out the ten cards below. Put a first-part card next to a last-part card to build a real science word. Write down every real word you can build, then write what it means.
Careful: some pairs make a word that sounds real but is not used in science. If you are not sure, mark it with a ? and check it.

blocks.label: Which card did you use the most? Why is it useful in so many science words?

blocks.a: Read one word you built and say what each part means.
blocks.c: Pick one word you built and explain how the two parts fit the science meaning.
blocks.e: Build one word you have never seen before. Predict what it might mean, then check it.

activities.title: Decode It: Hydrosphere
activities.description: Students use HYDRO and SPHERE to predict the meaning of hydrosphere, then check the prediction against a short science passage and revise if needed.

blocks.text: You may not know this word yet. Use the word parts to make a prediction, then read the science and decide whether your prediction still works.

blocks.label: Step 2: Predict. What do you think HYDROSPHERE means?

blocks.title: Step 3: Check the science
blocks.text: Earth's water is not only in the ocean. Water sits in lakes and rivers, moves underground through soil and rock, freezes into glaciers and ice caps, and floats in the air as water vapor. Scientists group all of this water together and call it the hydrosphere.

blocks.label: Step 4: Explain. Was your prediction close? Write the meaning of HYDROSPHERE using the passage.
Which of these are part of the hydrosphere? Check all that the passage supports.

blocks.a: What does HYDRO tell you?
blocks.c: Which sentence in the passage best supports your meaning?
blocks.e: What might HYDROELECTRIC mean? Which part gave you the clue?

activities.title: Decode It: Atmosphere
activities.description: Students decode atmosphere, then use the shared word part SPHERE to sort four of Earth's major systems and explain how one observation involves two of them.

blocks.text: Four science words share the same last part. Use that shared part, plus the first part of each word, to work out what each one names.

blocks.title: Read the science
blocks.text: Earth's systems are separated for study, but they touch each other constantly. The atmosphere is the layer of gases held around Earth by gravity. Warm air rising off the ocean carries water vapor upward. The vapor cools, condenses into clouds, and later falls as rain onto soil and rock, where plant roots take it in.

blocks.label: The passage describes rain falling on soil. Which two systems is that? Explain how you decided.
A student says the atmosphere and the hydrosphere never touch. Use the passage to explain why that is not correct.

blocks.a: Say what SPHERE tells you in all four words.
blocks.c: Explain how the first part of each word changes which system it names.
blocks.e: A LITHOSPHERE is another Earth system. LITH means rock. Which system you already know is it most like?

activities.title: Word Equation: Thermometer
activities.description: Students complete word equations for thermometer and speedometer, then separate the word-part clue from the full science meaning.

blocks.text: A word equation shows the pieces adding up to a whole word. Fill in the missing pieces. Then write the science meaning — it is usually more than just the two parts added together.
The word-part clue and the science meaning are not the same thing. A thermometer does not measure heat itself — it measures temperature. The clue got you close. The science makes it exact.

blocks.label: Look at the note above. Why is "a heat measurer" a good clue but not a perfect definition?
GEOTHERMAL uses THERM too. GEO means Earth. What do you predict GEOTHERMAL means?

blocks.a: What does METER tell you at the end of a word?
blocks.c: How does THERM fit what a thermometer actually does?
blocks.e: Invent a measuring tool. Name it with METER and explain what it would measure.

activities.title: Word Equation: Microscope, and the MICRO Problem
activities.description: Students build microscope and telescope from parts, then meet a word where MICRO does not mean what they expect — teaching that word parts are clues, not guarantees.

blocks.text: Complete each word equation. Then look carefully at the last section: one word does not follow the pattern.

blocks.caption: Odd word out
blocks.prompt: Three of these words use MICRO to mean small. One is different. Circle the one that is different.

blocks.label: Why is that word different? What does this teach you about using word parts?

blocks.text: Word parts give you clues. They do not give you guarantees. A good scientist checks the clue against the science.

blocks.a: What do MICRO and MACRO mean?
blocks.c: Explain why a microscope and a telescope share the part SCOPE even though they look at very different things.
blocks.e: Something is described as MACROSCOPIC. Do you need a tool to see it? Explain.

activities.title: Word Detective: Photosynthesis
activities.description: Students read an original observation passage, find science words, break them apart, predict meanings, and revise their predictions using evidence from the text.

blocks.text: Read the passage. Find the science words that are underlined. For each one, fill in the detective table: what parts do you recognize, what do you predict, what evidence did you find, and what is your final meaning?

blocks.title: Observation notes: the closet plant
blocks.text: Two bean plants started the same. Plant A stayed on a sunny windowsill. Plant B went into a dark closet. Both got the same water. After two weeks, Plant A was taller and dark green. Plant B was pale, thin, and leaning toward the door. Under a hand lens the leaves of Plant A were thick; the leaves of Plant B were thin and papery. The class had learned that plants make their own food through PHOTOSYNTHESIS, and that leaves have MICROSCOPIC openings that let gases move in and out.

blocks.label: Plant B had water but still did not grow well. Use the word parts of PHOTOSYNTHESIS to explain why.
The passage says the leaf openings are MICROSCOPIC. Why did the class need a tool to study them?

blocks.a: Break PHOTOSYNTHESIS into its three parts and say what each one means.
blocks.c: How do the parts of the word match what actually happened to Plant A and Plant B?
blocks.e: Predict what would happen to a third plant kept in dim light for two weeks. Explain using both the word parts and the evidence.

activities.title: Sort It: Herbivore, Carnivore, Insectivore
activities.description: Students sort animals by what they eat using the shared suffix VORE, then connect the sort to the direction energy moves in a food chain.

blocks.text: All three words end in VORE. Use the first part of each word to decide where each animal belongs. Write the animal in the correct column.

blocks.label: Which animal in the chain is a herbivore? How do you know from the word part?
The frog eats insects. Is the frog a carnivore, an insectivore, or both? Explain your thinking.
If the grasshoppers disappeared, what would happen to the frogs? Use the chain as evidence.

blocks.a: What does VORE tell you at the end of a word?
blocks.c: Explain how each animal's place in the food chain matches its VORE word.
blocks.e: An OMNIVORE eats plants and animals. OMNI means all. Which animals could be omnivores? Explain.

activities.title: Mystery Words: Earth and Space
activities.description: Four mystery-word cards give students clues but not answers. Students predict a meaning, name the strongest clue, and check it against a short science sentence.

blocks.text: Each card shows a mystery word and the clues inside it. Predict the meaning, circle the clue that helped you most, then read the science line and decide whether to keep or change your prediction.

cards.science: It gathers light from objects that are very far away.
It studies the objects in space and the patterns in how they move.
It is Earth's solid rock and soil, at the surface and far below it.
It is the layer found beneath the darker topsoil, with more clay and small rocks.

blocks.label: Which mystery word was easiest to predict? Why did the clues work so well for that one?
Which one needed the science line to get right? What did the science line add?

blocks.a: Choose one card and say both clues in your own words.
blocks.c: Explain how the two clues fit together to make the science meaning.
blocks.e: SUBSURFACE uses SUB too. Where would you look for something subsurface?

activities.title: Exit Ticket: Word-Part Check (BOY)
activities.description: A quarter-page beginning-of-year ticket. Students name what a word part means and say what clue it gives them. Four tickets print per page.

blocks.text: Answer in your own words. One or two sentences is enough.

blocks.label: MICRO means
So MICROORGANISM probably means
What clue did MICRO give you?

activities.title: Exit Ticket: Context Connection (MOY)
activities.description: A half-page middle-of-year ticket. Students connect word parts to a one-sentence observation and cite the evidence they used. Two tickets print per page.

blocks.title: Observation
blocks.text: A puddle on the playground shrinks all morning. By afternoon, clouds have formed overhead.

blocks.label: HYDRO means water. ATMO means air. Which word parts help you explain the observation?
Explain what happened, using at least one word part and the observation as evidence.

activities.title: Decode the Stimulus: Geothermal (EOY)
activities.description: The flagship end-of-year transfer task. Students meet an unfamiliar term, decode it, test the prediction against a diagram and a data table, then apply the idea to a new town.

blocks.text: You have not studied this word in class. Work through all five steps. Use the word parts and the evidence together — neither one is enough by itself.

blocks.label: Step 1: Break it. What word parts do you recognize, and what does each one mean?
Step 2: Predict. What might GEOTHERMAL mean?

blocks.title: Step 3: Check the science
blocks.caption: A cross-section of the ground beneath a small town. Water moves down through cracks in the rock, is heated by hot rock below, and rises back to the surface as hot water and steam.

blocks.label: Step 4: Explain. What evidence in the diagram and the table supports or changes your prediction? Write your final meaning of GEOTHERMAL.

blocks.stem: A town wants to heat its buildings without burning fuel. Based on the diagram and the table, which plan makes the most sense?
options: Pump water down to hot rock, then bring the heated water back up to the buildings.
Store cold water at the surface until the Sun warms it.
Leave barrels of water on the surface overnight and use them in the morning.
Move the town to a place with warmer weather.

blocks.label: Step 5: Extend. HYDROELECTRIC power uses moving water instead of heat. Both are called RENEWABLE. What do you think RENEWABLE means, and why do both belong in that group?

blocks.a: Say what GEO and THERM mean.
blocks.c: Point to one piece of evidence in the table that supports your meaning.
blocks.e: Another town sits on rock that warms only slightly with depth: 20 °C at the surface and 32 °C at 1,500 meters. Would a geothermal plan work as well there? Use evidence to explain.

activities.title: Break It: Cytoplasm
activities.description: Students break two CYTO words into parts, record what each part means, and see that CYTO always points to a cell.

blocks.text: Both words below share a first part. Break each word apart, write what each piece means, then say what the whole word means in your own words.

blocks.label: Both words begin with CYTO. What do both words have to do with?
A scientist studies diseased cells under a microscope. Which of the two words names that work, and how do you know?

blocks.a: Say what CYTO means in your own words.
blocks.c: Explain how the second part changes what each word is about.
blocks.e: Name one more thing you might study inside a cell. What could you call the study of it?

activities.title: Break It: Chlorophyll
activities.description: Students break CHLOROPHYLL and CHLOROPLAST, connect the green pigment to the structure that holds it, and generalize CHLORO to green.

blocks.text: Both words share the first part CHLORO. Break each word apart and write what each piece means.

blocks.label: Both words begin with CHLORO. What colour do you expect to be involved, and where?
Chlorophyll is held inside the chloroplast. Use the word parts to explain how the two are related.

blocks.a: Say what CHLORO tells you at the start of a word.
blocks.c: Explain how PHYLL and PLAST point to different things in the same green system.
blocks.e: Chlorine gas is pale green. Why might it share the CHLORO root?

activities.title: Sort It: Autotroph or Heterotroph
activities.description: Students sort living things by how they get food, using AUTO (self) and HETERO (other) to reason about the shared root TROPH.

blocks.text: Both key words end in TROPH, which is about feeding. Sort each living thing into the column that fits how it gets its food.

blocks.caption: Sort by how it gets food

blocks.label: TROPH appears in both words. What does that tell you both words are about?
A Venus flytrap makes food by photosynthesis but also traps insects. Why is it hard to place in just one column?

blocks.a: Say what TROPH means.
blocks.c: Explain how AUTO and HETERO change the way a living thing feeds.
blocks.e: Name one autotroph and one heterotroph in a schoolyard, and say how each gets its food.

activities.title: Word Equation: Endothermic and Exothermic
activities.description: Students complete word equations for endothermic and exothermic, then use the direction word part to decide which way heat moves.

blocks.text: Fill in the missing pieces of each equation. Then use the parts to decide which way heat moves in each change.
The direction part tells you which way heat moves, not the temperature you feel. In an endothermic change the surroundings give up heat to the change, so the surroundings feel colder.

blocks.label: An instant cold pack feels cold when you squeeze it. Which word describes it, and which way does heat move?
A hand warmer feels hot. Which word, and which way does heat move?

blocks.a: Say what ENDO and EXO mean.
blocks.c: Explain how the direction part matches what your hand feels.
blocks.e: Ice melting takes in heat from the room. Endothermic or exothermic? Explain.

activities.title: Decode It: Lithosphere
activities.description: Students break LITHOSPHERE, predict its meaning from the parts, then use the -SPHERE family to reason about other Earth layers.

blocks.text: Break the word, predict what it means, then check your idea against the note.

blocks.label: Break it: what does each part mean?
Predict: what do you think the lithosphere is?

blocks.text: The lithosphere is the solid, rocky outer layer of the Earth — the crust and the top of the mantle. It is cracked into plates that move slowly.

blocks.label: HYDROSPHERE and ATMOSPHERE also end in SPHERE. Using their first parts, what material do you expect each to be made of?

blocks.a: Say what LITH and SPHERE mean.
blocks.c: Explain how the two parts add up to the meaning of lithosphere.
blocks.e: Invent a name ending in SPHERE for the layer of living things on Earth. What first part would you use?

activities.title: Decode It: Isotope
activities.description: Students decode ISOTOPE, then use a data table of carbon atoms to work out what stays the same and what changes.

blocks.text: Break the word and predict its meaning. Then use the data table to check and finish your idea.

blocks.label: Break it: what do the parts mean?
Predict: isotopes sit in the same place on the periodic table. What might be the same about them, and what might differ?
What stays the same across the three atoms? What changes? Write your final meaning of ISOTOPE.

blocks.stem: Why are all three atoms still carbon?
options: They all have the same number of protons.
They all have the same number of neutrons.
They all have the same total mass.
They were all made at the same time.
blocks.followUp: What evidence in the table supports your choice?

blocks.a: Say what ISO means.
blocks.c: Explain how the table shows what is 'equal' about isotopes.
blocks.e: Two atoms of oxygen have 8 protons but different neutron counts. Are they isotopes? How do you know?

activities.title: Sort It: Intra or Inter
activities.description: Students sort descriptions by INTRA (within one cell) and INTER (between cells), then generalize the two prefixes to everyday words.

blocks.text: INTRA and INTER look almost the same but mean different things. Sort each description into the column that fits.

blocks.caption: Within one cell, or between cells?
items: a signal passed from one cell to the next

blocks.label: Explain the difference between INTRA and INTER in your own words.
Interstate highways run between states. Does that fit INTER? Explain.

blocks.a: Say what INTRA and INTER mean.
blocks.c: Explain how one letter changes intracellular into intercellular.
blocks.e: Give one everyday INTER word and one INTRA word, and say what each means.

activities.title: Word Equation: Hydrolysis
activities.description: Students build HYDROLYSIS from HYDRO and LYSIS, then connect it to how digestion breaks large molecules apart with water.

blocks.text: Complete the equation. Then use the note and your own words to explain what hydrolysis does.
Hydrolysis uses a water molecule to split a larger molecule into smaller pieces. Your body uses it to break food apart during digestion.

blocks.label: Which part of HYDROLYSIS tells you what does the breaking?
During digestion, a starch molecule is broken into sugars with the help of water. Explain how the word HYDROLYSIS matches that.

blocks.a: Say what HYDRO and LYSIS mean.
blocks.c: Explain how the two parts describe what happens to a large molecule.
blocks.e: ANALYSIS also ends in LYSIS. What idea of 'breaking apart' fits when you analyse a problem?

activities.title: Word Detective: Inside the Cell
activities.description: Students read original lab notes, break out CYTOPLASM and SEMIPERMEABLE, and revise their predictions using evidence from the text.

blocks.text: Read the lab notes. For each underlined word, fill in the detective table: the parts you recognize, your prediction, the evidence, and your final meaning.

blocks.title: Lab notes: the onion skin
blocks.text: A student peeled a thin, clear layer from an onion and placed it on a slide. Under the microscope, each block-shaped cell was filled with clear CYTOPLASM. A drop of coloured dye slowly moved into some cells but not others, because the cell membrane is SEMIPERMEABLE. The onion skin had no green colour, so the student knew these cells held little or no chlorophyll.

blocks.label: The dye entered some cells but not others. Use the parts of SEMIPERMEABLE to explain why.
The onion skin was not green. What does that tell you about chlorophyll in these cells?

blocks.a: Break CYTOPLASM into its two parts and say what each means.
blocks.c: How do the parts of SEMIPERMEABLE match what the dye did?
blocks.e: Predict what would happen to the dye if the membrane let everything through. What word would describe that membrane?

activities.title: Word Detective: Earth's Systems
activities.description: Students read an original passage about a rainstorm, then decode the four -SPHERE systems and track how one event touches all of them.

blocks.text: Read the passage. For each underlined word, fill in the detective table. Use the shared part SPHERE and the different first parts.

blocks.title: One storm, four systems
blocks.text: Clouds build over a valley and rain begins to fall. The water starts in the ATMOSPHERE. It lands on bare rock and soil, part of the LITHOSPHERE, and runs downhill into a stream that joins the HYDROSPHERE. Along the way, plant roots and thirsty animals in the BIOSPHERE take up some of the water. A single storm moves water through all four systems.

blocks.label: The four words share SPHERE. What does the first part of each one tell you?
Trace one raindrop through the passage. Name each system it passes through, in order.

blocks.a: Say what SPHERE means, and give one first part with its meaning.
blocks.c: Explain how the first part changes which Earth system each word names.
blocks.e: A wildfire sends smoke into the air and burns plants. Which two spheres does it touch? Use the word parts to explain.

activities.title: Sort It: One or Many
activities.description: Students sort words by MONO (one) and POLY (many), building number sense that carries into monomer and polymer.

blocks.text: MONO means one and POLY means many. Sort each word into the column its first part points to.

blocks.caption: One, or many?
items: a long chain of repeating units

blocks.label: MONOMER and POLYMER share the part MER, meaning unit. How does the first part change each word's meaning?
Carbon monoxide has one oxygen. How does its name fit MONO?

blocks.a: Say what MONO and POLY mean.
blocks.c: Explain how a polymer is built from monomers, using the parts.
blocks.e: Invent a MONO word and a POLY word for the classroom, and say what each would mean.

activities.title: Exit Ticket: Morphology Check (BOY)
activities.description: A quarter-page beginning-of-year ticket. Students name what CYTO means and use it to predict CYTOPLASM. Four print per page.

blocks.text: Answer in your own words. One or two sentences is enough.

blocks.label: CYTO means
So CYTOPLASM probably means
What clue did CYTO give you?

activities.title: Decode the Stimulus: The Selective Membrane (MOY)
activities.description: A mid-year decode task. Students meet SEMIPERMEABLE, break it apart, then test their prediction against a table of what crossed a membrane.

blocks.text: You may not have studied this word. Break it, predict its meaning, then use the table to check and finish your idea.

blocks.label: Break it: what does each part mean?
Predict: what do you think a semipermeable membrane does?

blocks.caption: What passed through the membrane after one hour

blocks.label: What kind of particle passed through? What kind was blocked? Write your final meaning of SEMIPERMEABLE.

blocks.stem: Why is the membrane called semipermeable and not just permeable?
options: It lets some things through but not others.
It lets everything through.
It blocks everything.
It only works for one hour.
blocks.followUp: Which rows in the table support your answer?

blocks.a: Say what SEMI means.
blocks.c: Explain how the table shows the membrane is only partly permeable.
blocks.e: A cell needs water but must keep large molecules in. Why is a semipermeable membrane useful to it?

activities.title: Mystery Science Word (EOY): Chemosynthesis
activities.description: The end-of-year transfer task. Students meet an unstudied word, decode it, test it against a deep-sea passage, and compare it with photosynthesis.

blocks.text: You have not studied this word in class. Work through every step. Use the word parts and the passage together — neither is enough alone.

blocks.label: Step 1: Break it. What word parts do you recognize, and what does each mean?
Step 2: Predict. What might CHEMOSYNTHESIS mean?

blocks.title: Step 3: Check the science
blocks.text: At the bottom of the ocean, no sunlight reaches. Yet around cracks in the sea floor that release hot, chemical-rich water, whole communities of tube worms and bacteria thrive. The bacteria do not use light. They build their food using energy released from chemicals in the water, and the tube worms depend on them.

blocks.label: Step 4: Explain. Using the word parts and the passage, write your final meaning of CHEMOSYNTHESIS.

blocks.stem: How is chemosynthesis different from photosynthesis?
options: It uses energy from chemicals instead of energy from light.
It uses light instead of chemicals.
It does not make food at all.
It only happens in plants.
blocks.followUp: What in the passage supports your choice?

blocks.a: Say what CHEMO tells you, and how it differs from PHOTO.
blocks.c: Point to one line in the passage that supports your meaning.
blocks.e: A microbe lives deep in a cave with no light but plenty of sulfur chemicals. How does it most likely make food? Use both the parts and the evidence.

activities.title: Partner Challenge: Build and Trade
activities.description: Partners take turns building a science word from cut-out parts and challenging each other to break it back apart and predict the meaning.

blocks.text: Work with a partner. Cut out the parts. Take turns: one partner builds a science word from two or more parts; the other breaks it back apart and predicts the meaning. Check each other with the word bank.

blocks.label: Which built word was the hardest to predict? Why?

blocks.a: Say which two parts made the clearest word you built.
blocks.c: Explain how you used the parts to predict a meaning you had not been taught.
blocks.e: Build one more word using a part not on a card. Challenge your partner to break it.

activities.title: Decode It: Kinetic Energy
activities.description: Students decode KINETIC from its parts, then use a data table of a cart's speed and energy to work out that kinetic energy depends on motion.

blocks.text: Break the word and predict its meaning. Then use the data table to check your idea and finish it.

blocks.label: Break it: what does each part mean?
Predict: what do you think kinetic energy is?

blocks.caption: The same cart at different speeds

blocks.label: What happens to the kinetic energy as the cart moves faster? Write your final meaning of KINETIC.

blocks.stem: A parked car has no kinetic energy. Why not?
options: It is not moving, so its kinetic energy is zero.
It is too heavy to store energy.
It has run out of fuel.
It is colder than a moving car.
blocks.followUp: Which idea from the word parts backs up your choice?

blocks.a: Say what KINET means.
blocks.c: Point to evidence in the table that kinetic energy depends on motion.
blocks.e: A bowling ball and a tennis ball roll at the same speed. Which has more kinetic energy, and why?

activities.title: Break It: Chromosome and Cell Bodies
activities.description: Students break CHROMOSOME and RIBOSOME, isolate the shared root SOME (body), and see how the first part names each structure.

blocks.text: Both words share the root SOME, meaning body. Break each word apart and record what every part means.

blocks.label: Both words end in SOME. What do the two structures have in common, based on that part?
Chromosomes were named 'coloured bodies' though they are not colourful in a living cell. Use CHROMO to explain where the name came from.

blocks.a: Say what SOME means at the end of these words.
blocks.c: Explain how the first part tells you which cell body is meant.
blocks.e: LYSOSOME also ends in SOME and comes from LYSIS (breaking apart). Predict what a lysosome does.

activities.title: Decode It: Mitosis and Meiosis
activities.description: Students break the two division words, then use a data table of chromosome numbers to connect MITO and MEIO to what each process does.

blocks.text: Break each word. Then use the data table to decide which process matches which set of parts.

blocks.caption: Two ways a human cell can divide

blocks.label: Which process reduces the chromosome number? How does its first part predict that?
MITO means thread and describes how the chromosomes look, not what changes in number. Why is MEIO the more informative name of the two?

blocks.a: Say what MEIO means.
blocks.c: Point to the row in the table that matches 'reduction'.
blocks.e: A cell must make gametes with half the normal chromosomes. Which process, and how do you know from the word part?

activities.title: Word Equation: Glycolysis
activities.description: Students build GLYCOLYSIS from GLYCO and LYSIS, then connect the -OSE sugar ending to glucose, the molecule that is split.

blocks.text: Complete the equation, then use the note and the parts to explain what glycolysis does.

Glycolysis is the first step of cellular respiration. It splits one glucose molecule into smaller molecules and releases a little usable energy. The sugar it splits, GLUCOSE, ends in -OSE, which marks a sugar.

blocks.label: Which part of GLYCOLYSIS tells you a sugar is involved? Which part tells you it is broken?
GLUCOSE, LACTOSE, and RIBOSE all end in -OSE. What do all three have in common?

blocks.a: Say what GLYCO and LYSIS mean.
blocks.c: Explain how the two parts describe what happens to a glucose molecule.
blocks.e: PHOTOLYSIS splits water using light. Using the parts, predict what is broken and by what.

activities.title: Sort It: Genotype or Phenotype
activities.description: Students sort descriptions by GENO (the genes carried) and PHENO (the traits shown), reinforcing the shared root TYPE.

blocks.text: GENO points to the genes an organism carries; PHENO points to what shows. Sort each description into the column it fits.

blocks.caption: Which does each describe?
items: the DNA sequence for a trait

blocks.label: Both words share the root TYPE. What does that tell you both words are describing?
Two plants show the same purple flowers but have genotypes BB and Bb. Explain how their phenotype can match while their genotype differs.

blocks.a: Say what GENO and PHENO mean.
blocks.c: Explain how one genotype can lead to a phenotype you can see.
blocks.e: A trait is hidden in one generation and reappears in the next. Which word explains why the gene was there all along?

activities.title: Word Detective: Homeostasis
activities.description: Students read an original passage about the body holding steady, then break HOMEOSTASIS and connect it to the evidence.

blocks.text: Read the passage. For each underlined word, fill in the detective table using the parts and the evidence.

blocks.title: Holding steady
blocks.text: On a hot afternoon a runner's body works to stay near 37 °C. As she heats up, she sweats, and the evaporating water cools her skin. Meanwhile her blood GLUCOSE rises after a snack, and her body releases a signal that moves the extra sugar into cells, bringing the level back down. Whatever the outside conditions, the internal state is pulled back toward a steady point. Scientists call this balancing act HOMEOSTASIS.

blocks.label: Using the parts of HOMEOSTASIS, explain why 'balance' or 'staying steady' fits better than 'no change at all'.
The passage describes two things being held steady. Name both, with the evidence for each.

blocks.a: Break HOMEOSTASIS into its two parts and say what each means.
blocks.c: How do the parts match what the runner's body does in the passage?

activities.title: Mystery Science Word (EOY): -ase and -ose
activities.description: The end-of-year transfer task. Students use two chemistry suffixes — -ASE for enzymes and -OSE for sugars — to decode unfamiliar biology terms they have not studied.

blocks.text: You have not studied these exact words. Use two reliable endings — -ASE for enzymes and -OSE for sugars — to work them out. Then check against the passage.

blocks.title: Reading the endings
blocks.text: In the small intestine, the sugar SUCROSE cannot be absorbed until it is broken into smaller sugars. An enzyme called SUCRASE does that job. The same pattern repeats elsewhere: the enzyme MALTASE breaks the sugar MALTOSE, and the enzyme AMYLASE breaks starch into sugars. The endings tell you which is which before you know anything else about them.
